description.value: Backcountry wilderness campground at Hummingbird Lake within South Chilcotin Mountains Park, a visually spectacular alpine setting of meadows, peaks and lakes roughly 150 km north of Whistler; no potable water (filter all sources), no staffed facilities, and grizzly bear encounters are not uncommon — full self-sufficiency required.

enrichment_extras.reasoning: The fetched website is the BC Parks page for South Chilcotin Mountains Park, the parent park containing this campground; no page specific to Hummingbird Lake Wilderness Campground was available. The park page explicitly states 'potable water is not available in the park' (negative evidence), confirms the park is a staffed-facility-free wilderness area, and confirms mountain biking is a permitted and supported activity on 200+ km of trails. All other amenity fields lack any confirming or denying evidence and are set to null.
concerns: The discovered URL resolves to the South Chilcotin Mountains Park overview page, not a page specific to Hummingbird Lake Wilderness Campground — campground-level details (site count, access route, reservations) are unavailable.
No phone number or physical address is recorded in OSM or on the website for this specific campground.
Park is described as having no staffed facilities and no regular ranger patrols — no amenities can be confirmed beyond what is explicitly denied (potable water).
Access route and road conditions to this backcountry campground are not described on the available page; suitability for loaded touring bikes is unknown.
enrichment_extras.recommended_status_reason: This is a primitive, unstaffed wilderness campground with no potable water and no on-site amenities; the only available web evidence is the parent park page with no campground-specific details. A reviewer should confirm that touring cyclists (not only mountain bikers on technical trails) can realistically access and use this site before including it in the directory.
enrichment_extras.notes: Mountain biking is explicitly listed as a permitted and supported activity in the park ('hikers, horse riders and mountain bikers'), and trail etiquette rules for multiple users including cyclists are spelled out. However, the park's primary cycling use case appears to be off-road mountain biking rather than road or loaded touring.
